---
title: "Project Knowledge Management"
---
This focuses on the continuous accumulation and organization of project knowledge, including context, decisions, methods, code, and data. The aim is to create an accessible history that enables others to effectively understand, reproduce, and engage with the work at any stage.

### Wikis
This involves maintaining a centralized, collaborative, and dynamic digital repository where team members can continuously document project context, technical methods, architectural decisions, and operational data. Characterized by interconnected pages and intuitive linking structure, a project wiki functions as a living archive that can be edited and searched in real time by all contributors. This framework ensures that historical context and technical institutional knowledge remain accessible and easy to update, preventing critical project insights from becoming siloed in individual communication channels or lost over time.

### Project Logs (Changelogs)
This involves maintaining a chronological, high-level journal that records major milestones, operational changes, and key direction shifts as the project evolves. Unlike dense meeting minutes, this running log extracts only the most critical historical events, such as when a new data source was integrated, a key script was rewritten, or a phase of work officially wrapped up. By skimming this centralized timeline, new team members can rapidly understand the project’s momentum and see exactly how past team actions led to the current state of the work. It serves as an efficient onboarding bridge that provides context without forcing newcomers to dig through months of administrative meeting records.

### Commit-driven documentation
This involves treating version control commit messages as a primary, real-time chronicle of a project's technical evolution and design rationale. By enforcing highly descriptive, standardized commit summaries, developers document the why behind every code change, bug fix, or architectural shift directly alongside the specific lines of code being modified. This framework transforms the repository's version history into an automated, immutable timeline, allowing future contributors to seamlessly trace the context and intent of the codebase without needing to cross-reference external, outdated documentation platforms.

### Readme Files
This involves placing a foundational text document at the very top level of your project repository to serve as the official welcoming guide for new contributors. This file outlines what the project does, lists the required tools to get it running, and provides step-by-step setup instructions to configure the environment. By keeping this onboarding guide accurate and updated, you eliminate friction for newcomers and ensure anyone can clone the project and begin working immediately. It is the single most critical artefact for making your work accessible and easily reproducible by outsiders.

### Architecture Decision Records (ADR)
This involves maintaining a running collection of short, text-based documents that record every major technical choice made during a project. Each record captures the specific problem you faced, the options you considered, and the exact justification for the path you ultimately chose. By keeping these documents directly in your project repository, you create an unchangeable trail of breadcrumbs that explains the "why" behind your technical setup. This artefact prevents future team members from accidentally overturning past decisions because they didn't understand the original context or constraints.

### Docstrings and Code Comments
This involves embedding explanatory text directly into the source code to document how individual software components work and why they were built that way. You use formal summaries inside functions to explain their inputs and expected outputs, while using short, casual lines of text next to complex code to explain tricky logic or workarounds. By keeping these notes right alongside the actual code, you ensure that the technical explanation stays perfectly synced with how the software behaves over time. This approach allows future developers to safely modify, fix, or reuse your work without having to leave their text editor to hunt for answers.

### Contribution Guidelines
This involves maintaining a clear instructional document that outlines the exact process and quality standards required for anyone wishing to add work to the project. This guide details how to format new submissions, how to run local testing suites, and how to successfully pass the team's review process. By establishing these ground rules up front, you ensure that external contributions match your existing standards without requiring constant, hands-on supervision. It acts as an intentional bridge that allows the project to scale smoothly while protecting the integrity of the core codebase.
